subject: Medicine
summary: Anaphylaxis is a rapid, systemic allergic reaction that can cause airway obstruction, circulatory collapse, and death if untreated. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria, with serum tryptase helping when the history is unclear.

sections.p: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life‑threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction that involves two or more organ systems or causes hypotension after exposure to a trigger.
b: Involves skin, respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal systems

t.b: Does the patient meet any of the three major criteria? Presence confirms diagnosis.
Is tryptase elevated above baseline? Supports mast cell degranulation when history is uncertain.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Ring and Messmer system, from mild cutaneous signs (grade I) to cardiovascular collapse (grade IV).
b: Grade II: Respiratory or GI symptoms

sections.p: Triggers are grouped by exposure type; food, insect venom, and drugs are most common worldwide, with additional considerations in low‑resource settings.
b: Infections (HIV, malaria) can act as cofactors

sections.p: Patients develop rapid skin flushing, urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, stridor, hypotension, and possibly loss of consciousness.
Testing supports diagnosis and identifies triggers; many tests may be unavailable in low‑resource settings, so clinical judgment is paramount.

t.b: Is mast cell degranulation present? Elevated level (>1.2× baseline) confirms reaction when history is vague.
Which allergen caused the reaction? Positive result guides avoidance; not needed for acute management.
Is there eosinophilia? May suggest allergic background but not diagnostic.

sections.p: Rapid progression to airway obstruction or circulatory collapse signals imminent death; delayed epinephrine increases mortality.
b: Severe bronchospasm unresponsive to inhaled bronchodilators

sections.p: First‑line is intramuscular epinephrine, followed by airway support, fluids, and adjunct medications. Treat underlying trigger after stabilization.
b: Epinephrine IM: reverses vasodilation, bronchospasm, and edema
Systemic corticosteroids to prevent biphasic reaction (adjunct)

sections.p: Patients need allergist referral, trigger identification, and an anaphylaxis action plan with self‑injectable epinephrine.
b: Educate on avoidance of known allergens

sections.p: Conditions that mimic anaphylaxis share respiratory or cardiovascular signs but lack the multisystem allergic trigger.
b: Vasovagal syncope (no skin changes, slower onset)
Acute asthma exacerbation (no hypotension, no urticaria)
Septic shock (fever, source of infection, gradual onset)

sections.p: Certain labs may be normal early or falsely elevated, leading to diagnostic uncertainty.
b: Serum tryptase may be normal if drawn >4 h after reaction
Baseline IgE can be high in atopic patients without anaphylaxis

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden difficulty breathing or voice change
Rapidly falling blood pressure or fainting
Severe swelling of lips, tongue, or throat

faq.q: Can anaphylaxis occur without skin symptoms?
faq.a: Yes, especially in children; diagnosis relies on respiratory or cardiovascular involvement after exposure.

faq.q: Why is epinephrine preferred over antihistamines?
faq.a: Epinephrine reverses life‑threatening airway and circulatory effects; antihistamines only treat cutaneous symptoms.

faq.q: When is a biphasic reaction likely?
faq.a: It can occur 1‑72 h after the initial event, more common after severe initial reactions or delayed epinephrine.

exam: List the three clinical criteria that establish a diagnosis of anaphylaxis.
Explain why intramuscular epinephrine is the first‑line treatment and describe its physiologic effects.
Identify two red‑flag features that require immediate escalation of care.
